image_description:
**1. Chart type**  
- **Faceted choropleth map** (four U.S. maps showing spatially encoded values with a diverging color scale)

**2. Layout techniques**  
- Uses **small multiples / faceting** in a **2×2 grid**
- Each panel represents a different **30-year period**
- No stacking

**3. Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location (U.S. area/region) | Spatial/geographic | Position on map |
| 30-year period (1901–1930, 1931–1960, 1961–1990, 1991–2020) | Temporal | Faceting into separate map panels; panel title; small timeline marker above each panel |
| Precipitation compared with 20th century average | Quantitative | Color/hue on map (diverging brown-to-teal scale); legend |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels on map |

comments.raw_comment: In observing the graphs, I noticed that as time progressed into the later part of the 20th century, heavier precipitation occurred. From the 1901-1930 graph, precipitation seems to have a concentration in the southwest plains area of the US. The overall least amount of precipitation seems to occur in the 1931-1960 graph. Then in the 1961-1990 graph, the occurrence of precipitation is wide spread, but not in high concentration. However, the 1991-2021 graph shows high concentration of precipitation in the Northwest and Midwest - this being the largest span covered so far. I wonder if this increase of precipitation has something to do with factors such as climate change, or the occurrence of natural disasters such as tornadoes or hurricanes due to geographical location. This increase relates to me and my community because I live in the Northeast's high concentration. This could be harmful to habitats and organisms but also increase the viability of certain organisms. The graph is depicting the United States' levels of precipitation in 30 year increments from 1901-2021. "Recent Precipitation Levels are Raining on the US's Parade"

text: In observing the graphs, I noticed that as time progressed into the later part of the 20th century, heavier precipitation occurred. From the 1901-1930 graph, precipitation seems to have a concentration in the southwest plains area of the US. The overall least amount of precipitation seems to occur in the 1931-1960 graph. Then in the 1961-1990 graph, the occurrence of precipitation is wide spread, but not in high concentration. However, the 1991-2021 graph shows high concentration of precipitation in the Northwest and Midwest - this being the largest span covered so far.

comments.raw_comment: Observing the graphs, I noticed the high concentration of precipitation during the period of 1991-2021 in the Northeast area of the country and a pretty low concentration of precipitation in the western area. During the time of 1931-1960, I noticed that there is the least amount of precipitation shown in the graph than there is in any other time period. The precipitation in 1901-1930 and 1961-1990, is more equally distributed in the areas rather than one heavier than the other. I wonder why some areas receive more precipitation in comparison to others and why precipitation has increased so much during the more current years. This relates to me and my community because in the more recent times, precipitation has been heavy in the northeast, which is where I live. This increase in precipitation can be harmful to some organisms by destroying their habitats or causing them to make changes to their lifestyles. It can also be beneficial because it reduces the amount of droughts and water shortages. The graph shows the amount of precipitation across America from 1901-2020, distributed by 30 year increments. The headline I would make for this graph is, "Precipitation in America: How Much is it Changing?"

•  Within a century, the precipitation in the US for the most part has increased considerably. Notably, the most current period from 1991-2020 has increases majorly in the eastern half of the US.

•  Precipitation can be both beneficial and harmful to the community, and is usually most harmful when in excess or lacking. Too much may cause flooding and its deadly impacts. Too little may cause agricultural barrenness, slowing food production for communities everywhere. 

•  Precipitation levels in the US are depicted in 30 year increments. Most notable are the periods 1931-1960 where there was considerably less precipitation, and 1991-2020 where there was considerably more. ("US Precipitation: Highs and Lows")

What is the cause of this heavy increase in precipitation (1991-2020) or even heavy decrease in precipitation (1931-1960)? Why do some places receive more/less precipitation than others?

•

sections.label: relate
text:
Precipitation can be both beneficial and harmful to the community, and is usually most harmful when in excess or lacking. Too much may cause flooding and its deadly impacts. Too little may cause agricultural barrenness, slowing food production for communities everywhere. 

•

sections.label: headline
text: Precipitation levels in the US are depicted in 30 year increments. Most notable are the periods 1931-1960 where there was considerably less precipitation, and 1991-2020 where there was considerably more. ("US Precipitation: Highs and Lows")

comments.raw_comment: When I analyzed the precipitation graphs, I noticed that there is a heavy dry concentration in the western states during the 1931-1960 period, and that for the northwestern group, their precipitation does not keep a significant pattern throughout the 120 year time period. I also noticed that in the most recent observed time period, the precipitation in the northeastern states is the most extreme it has ever been since being observed. After looking through the graph and information, I now wonder why the precipitation has had such extreme measures in the past few years and if there are any factors that may have caused it to be that way. These graphs relate to my location; I live in the northeast and I have observed in my past 16 years of living here that a lot of rain has been the standard weather for spring and fall months especially. This drastic change of precipitation has the ability to increase biodiversity in my area and in the northeast as a whole, which can be beneficial. In this graph, precipitation levels are being recorded and the extremity of the level correlates to a certain color on the map. I would make the headline of this graph "Why is it Raining So Much? What do you notice?
I notice that from 1901 to 1930, the relative precipitation is pretty evenly spread across the US. From 1931 to 1960, the relative precipitation is very low, with the most dry areas being around the Midwest and the Southwest. From 1961 to 1990, the relative precipitation is also pretty evenly spread, with maybe a bit more precipitation overall. From 1991 to 2020, the relative precipitation is very high, with most of it concentrated in the Northeast and the Midwest.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the precipitation levels fluctuate so much across the US?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Ever since I was born, I've noticed that it very rarely rains in Arizona, and I always wondered if Arizona was always like this. This data shows that Arizona wasn't always like this. Across the four time spans given in the graph, Arizona changes from having above average precipitation between 1901 and 1930, to having below average precipitation between 1931 and 1960, to having above average precipitation between 1961 and 1990, to having below average precipitation.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice from this data that the levels of precipitation have dramatically increased on the Eastern side of the country, making it have a more wet climate, while the Southwest, in contrast, has become more of a dry environment throughout the years. Thus, from 1901-60, most of the West and East seemed to have a drier climate than from 1961-2020, which shows the transition into the wet environment in the majority of the East.
I wonder whether global warming is a factor in this change in the climate. The warmer the air is, the higher the humidity and quicker evaporation of water which prompts tropical storms and hurricanes that have been occurring more lately. Another factor that may play into this is geography. For example, a state such as Arizona, with its canyons and deserts, already contains a dry climate, and global warming elevates that climate.

comments.raw_comment:
1. The first thing I noticed about this graph was that the change in precipitation between these years was very drastic. The biggest difference was between 1931-1960, and 1991-2020. In 1931, there was little to no precipitation, and now, there is a lot of precipitation. The graphs look like complete opposites. 
2. I wonder why that is the case. It was much dryer, and there was less rainfall in 1931 then there was in years past, and years afterwards, Why during that time was it so much dryer?
3. I remember two years ago, Andover was in a drought. It wasn’t a terrible drought but I remember hearing about it and how we couldn’t waste water. Things like these charts can affect anybody, because we are dependent on water for all sorts of everyday tasks.
4. “Droughting” the fact that the world is dry.

Title: "The Fall and Rise of Rainfall"

I noticed that over time, the areas that used to have more precipitation now have less, and the areas that used to have little precipitation now have more than they did in 1901-1930. It went from sparse precipitation in the west (1901-1930), to little precipitation nationwide (1931-1990), to heavier precipitation in the north and east.  One thing I wonder is if this was due to climate change or if it was just the course of weather patterns.

comments.raw_comment:
The precipitation levels have significantly risen over the past century. These levels have particularly increased on the east coast, around the New England area of the United States. The southwest is also currently experiencing much less participation than it did in the first half of the 20th century. 
How could the west and the east of the United States be impacted so differently in such a short period of time? How has human activity created such a drastic and fast impact on the earth and climate?
Climate change and specifically precipitation levels have huge impacts on communities around the world. In Portland Maine, we hardly feel the effects of climate change compared to other areas around the U.S. Although, we have experienced much hotter summers, and warmer winters as well. The snow this winter barely lasted and would melt quickly after snow fall.  In many communities increased or decreased precipitation has an incredible impact on agriculture and soil. This not only affects farms that grow produce for human consumption, but also the animals that depend on vegetation for their food supply.

comments.raw_comment:
The precipitation levels over the past century have changed drastically. For example, the 1901-1930 period had 3.0% to 6.0% precipitation levels in the midwest region. That seems to have flipped entirely in the 1931-1960 period, with precipitation levels reaching -6.0% to -9.0% in the same areas. The percentages seemed to even out mildly from the 1961-1990 period, with a general range of 3.0% to -3.0% across the country. 
Is it likely that global warming or advancement of industries are contributing to the change in climate? Why are Northwestern and Southeastern regions less visibly impacted than other areas? 
This issue is visible in my community, because Arizona's summer has dragged out quite a while. Dehydration is a prominent problem in our area, and several people are hospitalized due to their neglect of the situation. It's important to be informed about these statistics so you can better understand the effects it has on your community.

1.)I notice the graph shows how much precipitation the US gets during the years 1901-2001. Another thing that I noticed was that during the years 1931-1960 the US was drier and got less rain. In that graph, the place that gets the least amount of precipitation in the west. Lastly, the period that got the most precipitation was 1991-200. In that graph, it seemed the most precipitation occurred in the midwest, south, and northeast.

4.)The thing that is happening in the graphs is climate change and how is affecting our precipitation throughout the US. A good headline for the graph could be Climate Change VS Precipitation

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: Precipitation Takes Over In the United States 

I noticed that the participation increased after 30 years in some areas but also decreased in others. I find this interesting because the areas that look like they increased in 2020 are along the coast meaning the oceans could be getting warmer leading to more evaporation along the coast. In the years 1931-1960 the dust bowl took over much of the west leaving states in extreme drought around 80 years later it looks like the perception has flipped, leaving the US with high amounts of rainfall
What is this change due to? A lot of scientists refer to climate change as a major problem in our world due to the carbon dioxide breaking down the ozone layer and I am wondering how much has to do with climate change and how much has to do with other factors. This relates to my community because over this summer we experienced weeks of rain, it was mid July and there were rainfall records broken. I think change is bound to happen but this graph shows it over a drastic scale of time.

During 1901-1930, I was surprised to see that the western half of the US had the most precipitation. The reason why there is so little precipitation during 1931-1960 is most likely because of the dust bowl that occurred from 1930-1940, which was a period of extreme drought. In 1961-1990, it appears that the US had completely recovered from the dust bowl. In 1991-2020, the precipitation increased drastically across the US. I wonder if the extreme increase in precipitation is because of climate change. Additionally, I wonder what effect the increased precipitation has had on crops and agriculture. The main idea/title of this graph is: Precipitation in the US from 1901-2020

sections.label: notice
text: These four graphs depict precipitation over the years 1901-2021. In the first graph which shows the first 30 years, the precipitation levels were very different amounts in different hemispheres of the country. During this time also occurred the industrial revolution. Many pollutants were being released and this could've contributed to the weather being off from usual. Next in the 1930s to the 1960s that appeared to be a very dry couple of years. I do not know the exact reason behind this but I can assume that the pollutants had something to do with it. 1960-1990 there was a huge increase in precipitation levels.

sections.label: unprompted

comments.raw_comment: In these four graphs, you can see the incredible difference in precipitation over the years 1901-2021. During the early and mid-1900s, the precipitation levels were very different throughout the country. The US was booming with new industries and machines that had a big impact on the climate and precipitation. I also noticed that in the 1930s to 1960s there was a huge drought in the West and that was because in the 1930s the Dust Bowl took place. The Dust Bowl was an awful drought that hit the southern plains region and it lasted for almost a decade so that had a huge effect on the climate and the precipitation levels. In the 1960s to 1990s, there was a huge increase in precipitation and I wonder why there was such a big increase because the previous sixty years before some regions did not nearly experience that much rain. My thoughts are that the climate started to warm up and that caused a lot more precipitation. During the last thirty years, there has been a huge increase in rain and that is most likely because climate change has taken a huge toll on the earth all around. What I have noticed is that through the 20th century to the 21st century, the precipitation levels have been very different in all regions of the US. This relates to my community in many ways but mostly because we have been receiving a lot of rain in recent years. A catchy headline is “Precipitation and How it has Changed Over the Twentieth Century and Twenty-First Century”.

comments.raw_comment: In this series of data maps, I immediately notice that the East Coast blending into the middle of the country had an extreme increase in precipitation from 1990 to 2020. Another major change is in the 1931 to 1960 map where precipitation in the heartland decreased significantly from the thirty years prior. I wonder why precipitation had a major increase over the last thirty years, and why the rain slowly shift to the East side of the country? My second question connects to a point I made earlier, why did precipitation decline the most in the years 1931 to 1960? In the graphs, I think that precipitation increased more in the East rather than the West because of the colder, wetter weather that is more common on the East Coast. In the years 1931 to 1960, rain might've lessened because of the absence of available moisture in the atmosphere. I can connect these chloropleths to myself as well as my community because I live in New Jersey, on the East Coast. I am personally affected by the precipitation throughout the country, and even more specifically in town, for my school sports, outside events throughout the year, and storms that affect my surrounding area. A headline for this graph could be "Fluctuating Precipitation Levels and its Normality Over Time."

comments.raw_comment:
If you look at the four graphs all in chronological order, you can see how much rain increases from 1901 to 2020. But it doesn't start and stay in the same place. 1901 and the turn of the century observed lots of industrial demand, leaving more and more smoke and soot in the atmosphere all over the country. In this period the dust storms along with the Great Depression also occurred which once again reduced the amount of rain. In the 1940s, the West Coast seems to get drier while the midwest and east coast seems to receive more rain. However, it seems to even out between 1961-1990, but the southwest gets extremely dry from 1991 until now. 

These graphs make me wonder how much industrialization and globalization has influenced weather patterns. I would think that using more and more natural resources would cause drier weather patterns, so I wonder what caused such a major shift. 

This affects my community because I live in an area that floods easily, making just 3 inches of rain a concern.

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs, which are displayed as maps called choropleths, show the percentage change in average U.S. precipitation for three 30-year periods .  The data for these graphs are collected from over 15,000 weather stations around the country, including more than 8,000 stations operated by volunteers.  Volunteers have gathered data since 1890.  This is one of the oldest and largest citizen-science projects anywhere.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “How does this relate to you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

View our archives with free link: organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Sept. 24 with moderation on Wednesday, Sept. 29.  The topic:  2020 Census and state redistricting.  Keep noticing and wondering!

sections.label: unprompted
text:
Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs, which are displayed as maps called choropleths, show the percentage change in average U.S. precipitation for three 30-year periods .  The data for these graphs are collected from over 15,000 weather stations around the country, including more than 8,000 stations operated by volunteers.  Volunteers have gathered data since 1890.  This is one of the oldest and largest citizen-science projects anywhere.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “How does this relate to you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

View our archives with free link: organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Sept. 24 with moderation on Wednesday, Sept. 29.  The topic:  2020 Census and state redistricting.  Keep noticing and wondering!

In this graph I can notice how much the precipitation levels have risen in the U.S in the last 30 years. I can notice that there is a big difference in Iowa, that went from being not so dry, then very dry and then with a very high precipitation level. And in contrast, we can notice that Arizona was one of the states with highest precipitation levels in 1901-1930, and then in 1991-2020 became the State with more draught. 

I wonder if the north-east states of the United States will continue to have a higher precipitation levels in the future. I also have thoughts on whether Arizona is going to suffer lots of negative impacts due to draught and hot climate, for example, a lot of energy waste because of all the AC's that are probably going to be on daily use. Which means, there is probably going to be a rise in taxes causing more problems for people that don't have great jobs. 

This relates to me and my community in various ways, because if there are lots of crops in the places where the precipitation levels are high, that probably means there is going to be crops that drown, and that is not good for me and my community because it is probably going to be more expensive due to the reduction of the crops.

I can notice that there is a big difference in Iowa, that went from being not so dry, then very dry and then with a very high precipitation level. And in contrast, we can notice that Arizona was one of the states with highest precipitation levels in 1901-1930, and then in 1991-2020 became the State with more draught.

sections.label: wonder
text: I wonder if the north-east states of the United States will continue to have a higher precipitation levels in the future. I also have thoughts on whether Arizona is going to suffer lots of negative impacts due to draught and hot climate, for example, a lot of energy waste because of all the AC's that are probably going to be on daily use. Which means, there is probably going to be a rise in taxes causing more problems for people that don't have great jobs.

sections.label: relate
text: This relates to me and my community in various ways, because if there are lots of crops in the places where the precipitation levels are high, that probably means there is going to be crops that drown, and that is not good for me and my community because it is probably going to be more expensive due to the reduction of the crops.

text: "Precipitation levels increasing in the U.S"

The one thing I wonder from this graph is the cause for the 1921 to 1960 graph to have a low rate of precipitation. I assume that the Dust Bowl in the 30s played a part in it but I wonder if there were any other reasons.

This would impact my community because this could give a prediction of what the next 30 years of precipitation would be. 

Headline: Natural or Human Change.

Headline: Precipitation Takes Over In the United States 

I noticed that the participation increased after 30 years in some areas but also decreased in others. I find this interesting because the areas that look like they increased in 2020 are along the coast meaning the oceans could be getting warmer leading to more evaporation along the coast. In the years 1931-1960 the dust bowl took over much of the west leaving states in extreme drought around 80 years later it looks like the perception has flipped, leaving the US with high amounts of rainfall
What is this change due to? A lot of scientists refer to climate change as a major problem in our world due to the carbon dioxide breaking down the ozone layer and I am wondering how much has to do with climate change and how much has to do with other factors. This relates to my community because over this summer we experienced weeks of rain, it was mid July and there were rainfall records broken. I think change is bound to happen but this graph shows it over a drastic scale of time.

After viewing this graph, I noticed that the precipitation levels have gradually risen over the last 100 years. The graph says that precipitation levels have risen over 9% in the majority of the U.S. While I don’t know the exact reason for this gradual increase, I can infer that it is due to climate change and the melting of glaciers. The melting of glaciers causes an abundance of fresh water to be available for evaporation. 
        This is very concerning because if there is more water available and more precipitation, this can cause sea levels to rise therefore putting our future generations in danger. While I don't believe we can stop climate change and global warming, I think we can limit its impact on our earth. Our country can start by investing in renewable energy sources such as windmills, solar farms, and hydroelectricity. These are great methods for maintaining a steady climate.
